---
order: 3
unit: warmup
optional: true
title: Where a sentence starts
summary: "The start of a sentence tells the reader what it is about, and the rest adds something new. When each start picks up from what came before, the paragraph flows. Moving a time, a reason or a contrast to the start gives it the spotlight."
language: maths
node: [AC9E5LA04 n1, AC9E5LA04 n2, AC9E5LA04 n3]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "They picks up the penguins, which the reader already knows. Starting with After the storm picks up the storm and puts the time in the spotlight." }
hook: "Two sentences say exactly the same thing in different orders. Why does one fit the paragraph and the other make you stop?"
---
The **start** of a sentence tells the reader what the sentence is about. The rest of the sentence adds something **new** about it. When each start picks up something the reader already knows, the paragraph flows from one sentence to the next.

## Predict: which version fits?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to one of two same-meaning versions shows students already feel flow, before they can say why."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "'Wombats dig long burrows under the ground.' Which sentence fits best next?"
  options: ["Their burrows can be up to 30 metres long.", "Up to 30 metres is how long their burrows can be.", "Both fit equally well", "Neither fits"]
  actual: "Their burrows can be up to 30 metres long. It starts with what you just read about (burrows) and adds the new fact (30 metres). The other version starts with the new fact, so you have to hold it until the end to see what it is about."
```

## Try: choose the versions that flow

```step
stage: run
insight: "Choosing between versions with the same meaning isolates the one thing that changes: where the sentence starts."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#run", height: 330 }
hint: ["For each gap, look at the sentence before. Which version starts with something you already know?", "Starting with 'They' or 'Their' picks up the wombats. Starting with a new number or a new thing makes the reader wait."]
smaller:
  check: { type: question, q: "The sentence before is about wombats' burrows. Which start picks that up?", options: ["Their burrows...", "Up to 30 metres..."], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "30 metres is the new fact. Save it for the end."], explain: "Their burrows is something the reader already knows, so it makes a good start." }
check: { type: board, text: "Choose the version of each sentence that flows from the one before.", when: "n_gaps_right = 3", explain: "Each choice starts with something the reader already met (their burrows, they, these short legs) and ends with the new fact." }
```

Were you right about the wombat sentence? Every choice here followed the same rule: known first, new after.

## Worked example: follow the starts

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Reading only the starts of each sentence models how to check flow. Nib's slip is a sentence whose start jumps to something the reader hasn't met."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "'After the storm, the creek flooded the walking track.' What does putting After the storm first do?"
      options: ["It puts the time in the spotlight, so the reader knows when before what", "It makes the sentence a question", "It shows the storm was the most important thing in the whole text", "Nothing: the start of a sentence doesn't matter"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It is still a statement.", "It shows what matters in this sentence, not the whole text.", "Try reading 'The creek flooded the walking track after the storm.' The focus moves."]
      explain: "Moving the time to the start gives it the spotlight: the reader learns when first, then what happened."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Here is Nib's paragraph, one sentence per line. Click the sentence whose start jumps to something the reader hasn't met yet."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: start-with-new
      explain: "Line 3 starts with 'A sticky substance called propolis', which is brand new. Starting with 'They' (the bees) and ending with propolis would keep the thread: They seal gaps with a sticky substance called propolis."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why does starting with something the reader knows make writing easier to follow?"
      options: ["The reader connects the new information to what they already have", "It makes sentences shorter", "Teachers prefer it", "It means you never repeat a word"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Length doesn't change: the same words move around.", "It helps every reader, not just teachers.", "You often repeat or point back to a word to do it."]
      explain: "Known first gives the reader a hook to hang the new information on."
```

### Reading the starts

```worked
\text{Underline each start} :: Mark the first few words of every sentence, up to the main doing word.
\text{Read only the starts} :: Read them in a row. Do they follow a thread (wombats, their burrows, they)?
\text{Find a jump} :: A start that names something new breaks the thread. The reader has to stop.
\text{Move it} :: Rewrite so the start picks up something known, and the new thing comes at the end.
```

Now look at what a start can do when the writer moves a time to the front.

### Why known first?

## Vary: put it in the spotlight

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Choosing which part goes first for a reason (a time, a cause, a contrast) shows that the start is a choice the writer makes on purpose."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#vary", height: 300 }
hint: ["The first sentence after each gap tells you what the writer wants the reader to notice.", "If the surprise is that it happened despite the cold, start with Although."]
check: { type: board, text: "For each gap, pick the version whose start puts the right thing in the spotlight.", when: "n_gaps_right = 2", explain: "Although it was freezing puts the surprise first, and Because the bus was late puts the reason first, which is what each paragraph is about." }
```

## Practise: a paragraph that flows

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Three choices in a row on a new topic make the move a habit rather than a one-off."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#practise", height: 330 }
hint: ["Read the sentence before each gap. Which version starts with something already named?", "This paragraph is about the school's solar panels. Keep the panels, or what they make, at the start."]
check: { type: board, text: "Choose the version of each sentence that keeps the paragraph flowing.", when: "n_gaps_right = 3", explain: "Each choice starts with the panels or the electricity they make, so the reader never loses the thread." }
```

## Make: your own starts

In your own document, write a paragraph of at least four sentences about an animal, a place or a game. Make each sentence start with something the reader already knows.

Here is one example: "Our cat **Pepper** sleeps all day. **She** wakes up at dinner time. **Her favourite food** is tuna. **After dinner**, she goes out to hunt moths." The starts all pick up the cat or what the cat does.

Then read only the first few words of each sentence aloud, in a row, to a partner. Can your partner say what the paragraph is about from the starts alone?

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing a paragraph and then reading only its starts turns the check into a habit for their own writing."
hint: ["Choose an animal, a place or a game you know well and write four sentences about it.", "Read only the start of each sentence. Does each one pick up something from before?"]
check: { type: reflect, text: "I wrote a paragraph of at least four sentences, read only the starts aloud to a partner, and my partner could say what it was about." }
```

## In your own writing

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Rereading class writing for the starts of sentences is a quick edit students can keep using."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In a paragraph of my own writing, I underlined the start of each sentence and read the starts in a row. Where one jumped to something new, I rewrote it so the start picked up something the reader already knew." }
```

```teacher
summary: Students learn that the start of a sentence tells the reader what it is
  about, and the rest adds something new. When each start picks up something
  known, a paragraph flows. Moving a time, reason or contrast to the start puts
  it in the spotlight. Students choose between versions of the same sentence,
  find a start that jumps, and write a paragraph of their own and read its
  starts to a partner.
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 10 min · Vary 6 min · Practise 6
  min · Make and own writing 10 min
goals:
  - I can say what the start of a sentence tells the reader.
  - I can choose the version of a sentence that flows from the one before.
  - I can read the starts of my own sentences to check that my paragraph flows.
struggle: Both versions of each sentence are correct English, so students can
  feel there is no wrong answer. Ask them to read the paragraph aloud with each
  version and notice where they slow down.
before: >
  Do the Try board yourself: each gap offers the same sentence in two orders.


  The one idea: start with something the reader already knows, end with
  something new. This is the "theme" idea from AC9E5LA04 (sentence and paragraph
  starting points). You don't need the word theme with students; "the start"
  works.


  This is an optional warm-up from Year 5. Some of the "wrong" versions are
  passive (are run by, is used by). That isn't the lesson's point, but it's a
  good moment to notice that the passive can be useful when it puts the known
  thing first.
running:
  - "Predict: read both versions aloud. Which one makes you hold your breath?"
  - "Try: before each choice, ask what the reader already knows at that point."
  - "Worked example: read only the starts of Nib's paragraph aloud as a class.
    Where does the thread snap?"
  - "Vary: here the start is chosen to put something in the spotlight. What does
    each writer want you to notice?"
  - "Make: students write in their own document, then read only the starts of
    their own sentences to a partner."
stuck:
  - see: A student picks the version that sounds more interesting.
    ask: What did the last sentence end with? Which version starts with that?
    fix: Known first, new last.
  - see: A student thinks every sentence must start with the same word.
    ask: Does the thread need the same word, or just something the reader already
      knows?
    fix: They, their, these and a repeated key word all pick up the thread.
  - see: A student can't find the start of a sentence.
    ask: What is this sentence about?
    fix: The start runs up to the main doing word (the verb).
stretch: Take a paragraph from a science textbook. Underline every start. How
  many pick up something from the sentence before?
support: "A card: Known first, new last. Read the starts in a row."
leads: >
  Next in Holding writing together: repeating a key word on purpose.


  The starts of paragraphs (topic sentences) come later in the course, in
  Guiding the reader.
exit:
  q: "Which version fits after 'Our class grew sunflowers.': 'Taller than the
    fence they grew by March.' or 'By March, they were taller than the fence.'?
    Why?"
  a: By March, they were taller than the fence. The start puts the time first and
    picks up the sunflowers (they); the new fact comes at the end.
explain: >
  The **start** of a sentence tells the reader what it is about. The rest adds
  something **new**.


  A paragraph flows when each start picks up something the reader already knows:
  the same word, they, their or this.


  Moving a time, reason or contrast to the start (After the storm, Because the
  bus was late, Although it was cold) puts it in the spotlight.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: If two sentences mean exactly the same, can one still be better?
    prompts:
      - Better for whom?
      - Does it depend on what came just before?
    notes: "Yes: the better one depends on the sentence before it. On its own,
      neither is wrong. In a paragraph, the one that starts with something known
      flows."
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Starts only
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Show a short paragraph with everything hidden except the first three
        words of each sentence. Can the class say what the paragraph is about?
      notes: "If the starts follow a thread, they can. Try it with a paragraph that
        jumps: they can't."
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Read me your starts
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Pairs read only the starts of their Make sentences to each other. The
        listener says what the paragraph is about.
      notes: If the listener can't tell, the starts need to pick up a thread.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Spotlight
      type: question
      q: Which version puts the reason in the spotlight?
      options:
        - Because it was raining, the match was cancelled.
        - The match was cancelled because it was raining.
        - The match was cancelled.
        - It was raining.
      answer: 0
      explain: The reason comes first, so the reader meets it before anything else.
```

# Texts for "Where a sentence starts" (cohesion board). Each gap offers versions of the same sentence.

# region: run
widget: cohesion
p: Wombats dig long burrows under the ground. [[{Their burrows can be up to 30 metres long.|Up to 30 metres is how long their burrows can be.}=Their burrows can be up to 30 metres long.]] [[{They stay inside on hot days, where it is cool.|Cool places underground are where they stay on hot days.}=They stay inside on hot days, where it is cool.]] Wombats have short, strong legs. [[{These short legs are perfect for digging.|Digging is what these short legs are perfect for.}=These short legs are perfect for digging.]]
# endregion

# region: vary
widget: cohesion
p: The school swimming carnival went ahead on Monday. [[{Although it was freezing, every student swam.|Every student swam, although it was freezing.}=Although it was freezing, every student swam.]] Nobody expected that.
p: Half the class missed the start of the play. [[{Because the bus was late, they arrived after the first act.|They arrived after the first act because the bus was late.}=Because the bus was late, they arrived after the first act.]] The teacher has asked for an earlier bus next time.
# endregion

# region: practise
widget: cohesion
p: Our school put 40 solar panels on the hall roof last year. [[{The panels face north to catch the most sun.|North is the way the panels face, to catch the most sun.}=The panels face north to catch the most sun.]] [[{They make electricity whenever the sun is out.|Whenever the sun is out, electricity is made by them.}=They make electricity whenever the sun is out.]] [[{This electricity runs the lights and computers in the hall.|The lights and computers in the hall are run by this electricity.}=This electricity runs the lights and computers in the hall.]]
# endregion



# region: explain-pic
widget: cohesion
answer: on
p: [[Penguins|pen]] nest on the island. [[They>pen]] come ashore at dusk.
p: A big storm hit the island on Tuesday. [[{After the storm, the penguins stayed in their burrows for two days.|The penguins stayed in their burrows for two days after the storm.}=After the storm, the penguins stayed in their burrows for two days.]]
# endregion
